{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t)+5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Find an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above.

decisions.question: e-21654

source.question: e-21654
source.value:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/1e5a8eef63597c74566c624df6f52cf446c13d6d0ae16612b5ac3c45479f8816.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/9169c7aaf58e872a751777fffb26d435573ece6d79b1af64ccbe4b1bf6544463.png)

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $\mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+2y=0 \\ 5x+5y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one. So, we can disregard the second equation. 

From the first equation, we get

$$
2x+2y=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
2y=-2x
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
y=-x.
$$

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/72ee846ffe127bc7d4fb9e7b37b633f2c07e71f439c18471792e05fb56d0f7e1.png)

This determines the line with the equation $y=-x.$

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/cfff34f683e4c790f0f669a1babde2e9da9fcc10769c674f037ed3328d658f9f.png)

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

- First, notice that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/75c8006b52acb68b62c4f827fdd7b8c08709c647c7994f3088bf4f8f72eb3b8f.png) are the equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\dfrac13x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/c39f92243806a8682701374244fa2f7def32ab56ae509c920a31e75abfacb88f.png)

- Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/236a2688de746c23166d9159dfc073781ed55bc33cb289230f8bc9dbc00e323d.png) has the equation 
$y=- \dfrac12x$
and the straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/2527c2ffbb46a109eac9386b6b4bb634ca98768cf261252a2b94daf72f11a4a0.png)
lie on that line. Since $e^{-5t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/96a198c7fe3d98d3775ffc176b6659022b18676caf849cbc8d5c66833113bb19.png)

The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $\mathbf{v} = [3, \ 1]^T.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [-1, \ 0]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$  Sketch the phase portrait of the system.

decisions.question: e-21651

source.question: e-21651
source.value:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/32cdfec727ba37d7c21b4df53d40d29853c56a0bf7c5469227882de8bceb735a.png) 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}] & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3t-1 \\ t\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/810d48ff45c63e14ede1c9b7742298b263c861bba689595af6fe7afeac69f96d.png) are equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\dfrac13x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/bfc7b00f7f63aec120179da3f89f72f0aa53f13d299c95ed8f53e6238d329e51.png)

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/93ec8854dd09842895e8f0854683a03c2cae129198802f9b49c3d426179eb78b.png)
For example:

- When $c_1=1$ and $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=3t+2 \\ y=t+1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/55dfdfce480deba74fe46c1634e4c7ffb711fbd617525cdb5387bdabfc83ae75.png)

- When $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=-1,$ we get the following curve: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-3t-2 \\ y=-t-1\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add it to the phase space:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/2fb2297c741ea20ca729dcacb9934d7f8d1cca58af93c2b75db177890934b2b6.png)

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069892/assets/9e7970ba2d6bbe4745ee498cdbc72f2b7d8689219291847644bd6483696cc456.png)
